section.title: God and Idols
section.sectionRationale: Set among oracles of coming judgment, this chapter pauses to mock the whole enterprise of idolatry, a carved log dressed in silver and unable even to walk, and to praise the LORD who alone made heaven and earth. The chapter ends with Jeremiah's own prayer, caught between confessing that no one directs his own steps and pleading for correction tempered by mercy.
section.thesis: The nations' idols are worthless, man made, and powerless, but the LORD is the true and living God, Maker of heaven and earth, so that fearing anything else, whether carved images or one's own strength, is folly, and the only wise path is to entrust oneself to Him even in judgment.
section.frameNote: Four movements: a mocking exposure of idols as worthless, man made, and lifeless; a doxology praising the LORD as the true and living God who made all things; a warning of coming exile pictured as a collapsing tent; and Jeremiah's own prayer, acknowledging that no one directs his own steps and asking for correction with justice, not wrath.

units.label: Do not learn the ways of the nations
units.note: idols cannot speak, walk, or harm

verses.text: Hear the word that the LORD speaks to you, O house of Israel.

This is what the LORD says: 
“Do not learn the ways of the nations or be terrified by the signs in the heavens, 
though the nations themselves are terrified by them.
For the customs of the peoples are worthless; they cut down a tree from the forest; it is shaped with a chisel by the hands of a craftsman.

They adorn it with silver and gold and fasten it with hammer and nails, 
so that it will not totter.
Like scarecrows in a cucumber patch, their {{elil|idols}} cannot speak. They must be carried because they cannot walk. Do not fear them, for they can do no harm, and neither can they do any good.”

units.label: There is none like You, O LORD

verses.text: There is none like You, O LORD. You are great, and Your name is mighty in power.

Who would not fear You, O King of nations? This is Your due. For among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, 
there is none like You.
But they are altogether senseless and foolish, instructed by worthless idols made of wood!
Hammered silver is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz, the work of a craftsman from the hands of a goldsmith. Their clothes are blue and purple, all fashioned by skilled workers.
But the LORD is the true God; He is the {{chai|living}} God and eternal King. The earth quakes at His wrath, and the nations cannot endure His indignation.
Thus you are to tell them: “These gods, who have made neither the heavens nor the earth, will perish from this earth and from under these heavens.”

The LORD made the earth by His power; He established the world by His wisdom 
and stretched out the heavens by His understanding.
When He thunders, the waters in the heavens roar; He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth. He generates the lightning with the rain and brings forth the wind from His storehouses.
Every man is senseless and devoid of knowledge; every goldsmith is put to shame by his idols. For his molten images are a fraud, and there is no breath in them.
They are worthless, a work to be mocked. In the time of their punishment they will perish.
The Portion of Jacob is not like these, for He is the Maker of all things, and Israel is the tribe of His inheritance, the LORD of Hosts is His name.
Gather up your belongings from this land, you who live under siege.

For this is what the LORD says: 
“Behold, at this time I will sling out the inhabitants of the land and bring distress upon them so that they may be captured.”
Woe to me because of my brokenness; my wound is grievous! But I said, “This is truly my sickness, and I must bear it.”
My tent is destroyed, and all its ropes are snapped. My sons have departed from me and are no more. I have no one left to pitch my tent or set up my curtains.
For the shepherds have become senseless; they do not seek the LORD. Therefore they have not prospered, and all their flock is scattered.
Listen! The sound of a report is coming, a great commotion from the land to the north. The cities of Judah will be made a desolation, a haunt for jackals.

units.label: Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice

verses.text: I know, O LORD, that a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps.
Correct me, O LORD, but only with justice, not in Your anger, or You will bring me to nothing.

Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You, and on the families that do not call on Your name. For they have devoured Jacob; they have consumed him and finished him off; 
they have devastated his homeland.

elil.gloss: Worthless things, a mocking wordplay on el, god, that reduces idols to mere nothings. The same root gives Scripture some of its sharpest satire against false gods, calling them elilim, no gods at all, rather than granting them any real power.

chai.gloss: Living, alive. The LORD is repeatedly called the living God in contrast to lifeless idols that must be carried because they cannot walk; this same word roots Israel's confession that her God actually acts, speaks, and reigns.

basic.context: In the middle of oracles announcing judgment, Jeremiah pauses to mock the idols the nations trust: logs cut from the forest, decorated with silver and gold, nailed down so they will not fall over, unable to speak, walk, or do any good or harm. Against this parade of helpless statues, Jeremiah bursts into praise: there is none like the LORD, who made the heavens and the earth by His own power and wisdom. The chapter turns personal at the end, as Jeremiah himself prays, asking for correction tempered by justice rather than raw anger.
basic.hermeneutics: This is both satire and doxology in the same breath, exposing the absurdity of idol worship, carrying an object so it will not fall down, while exalting the living God who needs no one to hold Him up. The chapter's final prayer shows the prophet applying his own message to himself, confessing human dependence and asking for merciful discipline.
basic.originalLanguages: Jeremiah calls the idols elilim, worthless things, a biting wordplay on el, god, that reduces them to nothings rather than real gods. By contrast the LORD is chai, living, alive, active, the one true God whose wrath makes the earth quake, unlike idols with no breath in them at all.
basic.typology: The contrast between dead idols that must be carried and the living God who carries His people points forward to the true and living Word, Jesus Christ, who is not carried by human hands but who Himself sustains all things and, unlike any idol, actually rose from the dead.
basic.christ: John opens his Gospel echoing this chapter's praise of the LORD who made the heavens and the earth, applying that same creative power to the Word who became flesh, Christ, through whom all things were made, John 1:1-3. Where idols have no breath in them, Jesus is the resurrection and the life, breathing life into the dead rather than needing to be carried.
basic.god: God alone made the earth by His power and established the world by His wisdom; no other so called god shares in that work, and none will endure it. He is also personal enough that Jeremiah can bring his own fears to Him directly, asking for correction shaped by justice and mercy rather than unrestrained wrath.
basic.crossReferences: John 1:1-3 credits Christ with the same creative power praised here. Isaiah 44:9-20 gives a parallel satire of idol making. Psalm 115:4-8 warns that those who make idols become like them. Acts 17:24-25 echoes this chapter's logic that the true God needs nothing from human hands.
basic.oneStory: This is Scripture's ongoing contrast between dead things people make and the living God who made everything else, a contrast that runs from Eden's true worship through the prophets' satire of idols to the Word made flesh who is Himself the true and living God among us.

context.literary:
Jeremiah 10 sits inside the long temple sermon block that begins at 7:1, where Jeremiah is told to stand in the gate of the LORD's house and speak to those who come in to worship. Chapters 7 to 9 have been a litany of false trust: in the temple, in sacrifices, in the Queen of Heaven. Chapter 10 turns the camera from Judah's idols to the idols themselves. It is a small, tightly built piece of satire set inside a prophet's grief.

The unit has a clear shape. Verses 1 to 5 are a prophetic warning in the second person, and they close with a double negation, no harm and no good. Verses 6 to 10 break into praise addressed directly to God ('You'), which is unusual in a prophetic oracle, where the LORD normally speaks about Himself. Verses 11 to 16 then swing back to instruction and description, and verse 16 ends with the first mention of Israel since verse 1, so the section is framed by the people who are being warned and the people who belong to the true God. Verses 17 to 22 are a dirge, voiced partly by the LORD, partly by a mourning figure, and verses 23 to 25 are Jeremiah's private prayer.

Two small structural signals are easy to miss. The word for senseless, from one root, falls on the nations' wise men in verse 8, on every idol maker in verse 14, and on Israel's own shepherds in verse 21. The charge against idolatry is thereby turned into a charge against Judah's leaders. And verses 12 to 16 reappear almost word for word in Jeremiah 51:15 to 19, there aimed at Babylon. Jeremiah's hymn to the Creator travels, and near the close of the book it becomes a weapon against the very empire that will carry Judah away.
context.historical:
Josiah's reform had swept the land of astral cults and carved images only a few years before, 2 Kings 23:4-14, yet Jeremiah's sermons show the habits returning or never leaving: incense to the sun, moon and stars, Jeremiah 8:2, and cakes for the Queen of Heaven, Jeremiah 7:18. The 'signs in the heavens' of verse 2 are those astral omens. The Torah had already told Israel that the heavenly host were assigned to the nations and not to be worshipped, Deuteronomy 4:19, and the nations around Judah, above all Babylon, read their futures in the sky and trembled at eclipses and comets. Jeremiah's point is that Judah should not borrow a fear the Creator has no part in.

The picture of the idol in verses 3 to 5 is accurate to the workshop. A tree is felled, shaped, plated and fixed so it will not topple. Isaiah 40:19-20 and 46:6-7 describe the same trade, and Isaiah 46:1-2 shows Babylon's gods loaded onto animals, a burden to the weary beasts that carry them. Mesopotamian texts also record rituals in which a finished statue was washed and ritually 'opened' at the mouth so it could be treated as alive. Jeremiah's line that there is 'no breath' in the idol, verse 14, presses on exactly that claim.

The luxuries are named from the far ends of the known world. Silver from Tarshish is attested as a Phoenician trade good, Ezekiel 27:12, and gold from Uphaz appears again in Daniel 10:5. Blue and purple were the costliest dyes, and they were the same colours Israel had used in the tabernacle curtains, Exodus 26:1. Jeremiah sees the irony: the finest materials, which God's own sanctuary had used, are being spent to dress a thing that cannot move.

Verse 11 is in Aramaic, the language that Judah's officials already knew was the language of diplomacy, 2 Kings 18:26. The exiles who would soon live in Aramaic speaking lands were being given a sentence to say to their neighbours in their neighbours' own tongue.
context.canonical:
Few themes run through Scripture more steadily than the mockery of idols. It begins in the law, where the person who makes a carved image is cursed, Deuteronomy 27:15, and the first commandments forbid any likeness to be worshipped, Exodus 20:4-5. The Psalms sing it, Psalm 115:4-8 and 135:15-18, and Isaiah gives it its longest expression, Isaiah 40:18-20, 44:9-20 and 46:1-7. Jeremiah's own contribution is to place the satire in the middle of a funeral, so that the sneer is never light. In 16:19-20 he sees the day when the nations will confess that their fathers inherited nothing but lies, which turns this mockery into a prophecy of conversion.

The praise in verses 12 to 13 draws on the same stock of creation hymns that stands behind Proverbs 3:19-20, Psalm 33:6 and Psalm 135:7. Verse 13 is nearly the whole of Psalm 135:7. Verse 25 is close to Psalm 79:6-7, so either Jeremiah or the psalmist borrowed a liturgical cry, and in both settings a people who had been devoured asked God to answer.

The New Testament carries the argument straight on. At Lystra Paul tells the crowd to turn 'from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea,' Acts 14:15, and in Athens he says the God who made the world is not served by human hands, Acts 17:24-25. In 1 Thessalonians 1:9 conversion is described as turning to God from idols to serve the living and true God. Paul grants that an idol is nothing in the world, 1 Corinthians 8:4, while warning that what lies behind idolatry is real. Revelation 4:11 gives the creation praise of this chapter to the elders around the throne, and Revelation 15:3 gives the title 'King of the nations' to the God of Moses and the Lamb.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah wanted Judah to feel the foolishness of idolatry, not merely to be told it was forbidden. The picture of a god that has to be nailed down so it will not fall over is meant to make a listener laugh, and then to stop laughing when he realises he has been doing something like it. The prophet is doing what a good teacher does with a strong temptation: he takes away its glamour.

He also wants the fear of the LORD to push out every lesser fear. The first thing the people are told not to fear is not a statue but the sky, verse 2, so the passage is about what we allow to terrify us as much as what we bow to. A nation under siege, verse 17, will always be tempted to read omens and look to powers it can see. Jeremiah answers that the One who stores the wind and thunders over the clouds is the One who has spoken to them.

Finally, the prayer in verses 23 to 25 shows the prophet living inside his own message. He has just said that idols cannot direct anything; he now confesses that neither can he. The sermon ends with no triumph, only a man asking to be corrected gently, and that is part of what Jeremiah hoped hearers would copy.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes Judah's attraction to astral religion and the craft of idol making, and it records a prophet's own prayer. It does not tell believers to ask for the destruction of others as a general rule, and the closing request that wrath be poured on the nations has to be read as a petition from within a covenant under attack, one that Psalm 79:6-7 shares and that the New Testament never turns into a command, Romans 12:19.

What does carry forward is the pattern of discernment. Idols today seldom look like a log in a cucumber patch, but the test in verse 5 still works on anything that claims our trust: does it speak, does it move, can it do good or harm? Paul can say an idol is nothing, 1 Corinthians 8:4, and also say that people can still be ruined by what they exchange the glory of God for, Romans 1:23. The right response is not contempt for people but worship of the Maker, and a willingness to say with verse 23 that our own steps are not ours to direct.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verses 19 to 22: Jeremiah, the city, or the LORD?

views.label: Jeremiah the mourning prophet
views.case: The 'I' of verse 19 who is wounded and bears his sickness matches the prophet's laments elsewhere, Jeremiah 8:18-9:1 and 14:17. On this reading the tent, ropes and missing sons of verse 20 are the prophet's own language for the ruin of his people, and he shares their grief.

views.label: Jerusalem or the daughter of Zion personified
views.case: The voice of a mother whose tent is torn down and whose children are gone fits the way Jeremiah elsewhere gives speech to the city, Jeremiah 4:19-21, and Lamentations does the same. The pitched tent is an image for a household or a sanctuary, and the speaker is the wounded land.

views.label: A voice that moves between God, city and prophet
views.case: The oracle of verses 17 to 18 begins with God's word, verse 21 turns to the shepherds in the third person, and verse 22 is announced as a report. Some readers hear the speakers shifting without notice, a common feature of Hebrew poetry, so that God, people and prophet all grieve.

debates.bearing: The difference matters less than the shared fact. In each reading the judgment is received as a wound by someone who loves the people, which fits Jeremiah's habit elsewhere of weeping over what God has told him to announce.

debates.question: Why is verse 11 written in Aramaic, and does it belong to the chapter?

views.label: An original, deliberately Aramaic sentence
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that this verse is in Aramaic. Aramaic was the language of diplomacy, 2 Kings 18:26, and the verse reads like a slogan: gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish from them. Jeremiah may be handing the exiles a ready reply in their neighbours' language.

views.label: A later addition
views.case: Because verse 11 interrupts the Hebrew flow between verses 10 and 12 and is the only Aramaic verse in the book, some scholars suggest a scribe added it as a marginal comment. It is found in the Hebrew text that has come down to us, however, and nothing in its content conflicts with the chapter.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is right, the verse works as the pivot of the hymn. It states the thesis in the form of a rebuttal anyone can say, and the following verses explain it by describing the true Creator.

debates.question: Is the prayer for wrath on the nations in verse 25 a model for believers?

views.label: A legitimate petition within the covenant
views.case: The nations had devoured Jacob, and Israel is asking God as judge to answer. Psalm 79:6-7 makes the same appeal, and Revelation 6:10 records the martyrs asking how long before their blood is avenged. Jeremiah leaves the vengeance to God and does not take it himself.

views.label: A prayer that Christ's teaching reshapes
views.case: Jesus tells His followers to pray for those who persecute them, Matthew 5:44, and prays for His own killers, Luke 23:34. On this view the prayer records an honest feeling in an earlier stage of revelation that the New Testament redirects toward mercy.

debates.bearing: The two are not as far apart as they seem. Both leave justice with God, and Jeremiah himself has just asked to be treated justly rather than in anger. What Christ adds is that the same mercy God shows to His own is on offer to the nations that Jeremiah's prayer condemns, as the later chapters of this book hint, Jeremiah 12:15-16.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for 'worthless' in verses 3 and 15 is hevel, whose root meaning is breath or vapour. It is the word that Ecclesiastes 1:2 translates 'futility.' Jeremiah has already used it of Judah's own history in Jeremiah 2:5, where the fathers followed worthless things and 'became worthless themselves.' Placed beside Psalm 115:8 and 135:18, 'those who make them become like them,' the hint is that idolatry does not merely waste a person's time, it empties the person.

The verb 'learn' in verse 2 comes from the root that gives the word for a disciple or a pupil. 'Do not learn the ways of the nations' is the language of apprenticeship. Judah is picturing itself as a student of the surrounding world, and Jeremiah is saying that the curriculum is hevel. When he says in 12:16 that the nations may yet 'learn the ways of My people,' it is the same root pointed in the opposite direction.

Verse 14 says 'there is no breath in them.' The Hebrew word is ruach, breath or wind or spirit, the same word that Habakkuk 2:19 uses of an idol overlaid with gold and silver, 'there is no breath in it at all.' The statues have the most expensive skins and the least inside. The 'fraud' of that verse is sheqer, lie or deceit, the word Jeremiah uses all through the book for the false claims of false prophets, which links idol making to false speaking.

The three instruments of creation in verse 12 are power, wisdom and understanding. Proverbs 3:19-20 gives two of the three in the same order, so Jeremiah is quoting a settled way of praising God as Maker. Against a world that credited each cosmic force to a separate deity, the verse says one will and one intelligence made everything. The 'storehouses' of verse 13 make the weather a stored treasure, not the property of a rival god, and Psalm 135:7 sings the same line.

The 'Portion of Jacob' in verse 16 is a striking reversal. The word for portion is the share of an inheritance, and Psalm 16:5 and Lamentations 3:24 say that the LORD Himself is the believer's portion. The nations hold gods of their own manufacture, and Israel holds the Maker, while Deuteronomy 32:9 says the LORD's portion in turn is Jacob. Each belongs to the other.

Verse 18 says God will 'sling out' the inhabitants. It is the verb of a slinger hurling a stone, as in 1 Samuel 25:29, where Abigail says God will fling away the lives of David's enemies 'like stones from a sling.' Judah is to be flung from the land like a pebble. In verse 23 the phrase 'directs his steps' uses the same verb as Proverbs 16:9, where God 'determines' a man's steps. And 'correct' in verse 24 is the verb of discipline, used for a father's training of a child in Jeremiah 30:11 and 46:28, where God promises to discipline His people 'justly.' Jeremiah asks for exactly what God has said He will give.

typology.type: The idol that must be carried, Jeremiah 10:5
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 46:1-4 sets Babylon's gods, which burden the animals that carry them, beside the LORD who says He has carried Israel since birth and will carry them to old age. The contrast between a god carried and a God who carries comes to rest in Christ, who 'upholds all things by His powerful word,' Hebrews 1:3, and who bears His people's sins on the cross, 1 Peter 2:24. The type falls short because the pagan idols are mere objects, while Christ is a person who chooses to be carried to the cross, and then rises.

typology.type: The King of the nations, Jeremiah 10:7
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah praises the LORD as the King whom all the nations ought to fear. In Revelation 15:3-4 the redeemed sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, calling Him 'King of the nations' and saying that all nations will come and worship. Jesus is the Davidic king whose reign reaches to the nations, Matthew 28:18-19. The correspondence is that Jeremiah's claim about God's universal kingship is realised in a Messiah with a worldwide people. It remains incomplete until the nations Jeremiah speaks of in 16:19 actually arrive.

typology.type: The Maker whose power sets the weather, Jeremiah 10:12-13
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah calls the One who commands wind and storm the true God. In the Gospels Jesus stills a storm with a word and the disciples ask who this is, Mark 4:39-41, and Colossians 1:16-17 says all things were created through Him and for Him and in Him hold together. The pattern is that the Maker's authority over creation is now seen in a man. It is more than a pattern, since Jeremiah is not predicting the incarnation, but the New Testament reads the praise of the Creator as praise that belongs to the Son.

typology.type: The one who cannot direct his own steps, Jeremiah 10:23
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah confesses dependence and asks to be corrected justly. Jesus in Gethsemane prays in the same posture, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and Hebrews 12:5-6 tells believers not to despise the Lord's discipline because He disciplines those He loves. The difference is decisive: Jeremiah needs correction, and Christ needs none. He takes the full weight of wrath that Jeremiah begs to be spared, so that discipline for His people becomes the training of sons and no longer the sentence of a judge.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most directly by the claim it makes about who made the world. Jeremiah sets the LORD alone against every rival, and the New Testament writers do not hesitate to put Jesus on the Creator's side of that line. 'Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made,' John 1:3. 'All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together,' Colossians 1:16-17. These are not claims that the Son is a second creator beside God. They say that the God of Jeremiah 10:12 is the God now known in Jesus, and that the words 'by His power, by His wisdom, by His understanding' have a face. Paul even calls Christ 'the power of God and the wisdom of God,' 1 Corinthians 1:24, which gathers two of Jeremiah's three nouns.

The chapter also leads to Christ by the contrast of breath. The idols have none, verse 14. Jesus breathes on His disciples and says, 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' John 20:22, and claims 'I am the resurrection and the life,' John 11:25. Where a statue is carried into place and cannot answer when its worshippers call, Isaiah 46:7, Jesus walks, speaks, and raises the dead. The living God that Jeremiah praises in verse 10 shows His life by overcoming death.

Third, the fear that the passage opens with, the fear of omens and signs in the sky, finds its answer in the One who is Lord of the heavens. Those who had read the stars for warnings were told that the real sign in the heavens is the Son of Man, and the real fear is of Him, Matthew 24:30, which is a very different fear from dread of an eclipse.

Fourth, Jeremiah's prayer is answered in a way he could not foresee. He asks to be corrected 'with justice, not in Your anger.' At the cross God's anger against sin is spent on His Son, Romans 3:25-26, so that the discipline His people receive is the loving discipline of Hebrews 12:5-6 and no longer wrath. The man who cannot direct his own steps is finally led by the Shepherd who goes before His sheep, John 10:4.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Jeremiah's polemic is aimed at real idols in his own day, and he is not secretly describing Jesus when he says the idols cannot speak. The links are those the apostles themselves draw: Christ shares the creating work of God and is the living, speaking and breathing God against every dead thing, and He bears the wrath that Jeremiah can only ask God to temper.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who is incomparable without being remote. Verses 6 and 7 say twice, 'there is none like You,' and the reason given is not abstract: He is great, His name is mighty, and He is King of the nations, which means He owns authority over peoples who do not know Him. The word 'due' in verse 7 says that fear is owed to Him as a debt, not as a mood. Yet the same God is addressed in the second person and invoked as 'my' Lord by a man in pain, so the passage holds His majesty and His nearness in one breath.

God is the one living God, verse 10, and that adjective governs everything else. The idols are inert and must be moved; He moves. His anger is not a stage effect, since the earth quakes under it. Life, in Scripture, is an attribute of God before it is a gift to creatures, as John 5:26 puts it: the Father has life in Himself. Because He is alive He can act in history, which is why the exile is His doing, and not the victory of Babylon's gods.

He is Creator by wisdom. The triad of power, wisdom and understanding in verse 12 teaches that the world has an intelligible order that comes from a mind, so that the weather is not caprice and the stars are not rulers. God stores the wind and the lightning and sends them on His errands, verse 13, so even the fiercest forces of nature are on a leash. That makes verse 2 reasonable: if the heavens answer to Him, nothing in the heavens deserves our terror.

He is faithful to the people He calls His portion. Verse 16 does not say Israel is better than the nations; it says the LORD has made them His inheritance, as Deuteronomy 32:9 states. Judgment in verses 17 to 22 therefore falls on His own household, and that is why it is lamented. He slings out the inhabitants of the land, verse 18, and yet the one who tells Jeremiah to proclaim it is also the God whose prophet weeps.

He disciplines justly. The prayer in verse 24 assumes that God's correction can be measured by justice and that His anger need not be the whole of His response. Jeremiah 30:11 makes the promise explicit: 'I will discipline you justly,' alongside the pledge that He will not destroy His people completely. God is neither indifferent to sin nor blindly furious.

For worship, the chapter calls us to name what we trust and put it beside the Maker. It invites fear as an act of worship, 'Who would not fear You?', and it invites dependence as the fruit of the knowledge that no one directs his own steps. The right response is the praise of verses 6 and 7 and the humble prayer of verse 24 together.

crossReferences.note: These verses repeat the hymn of Jeremiah 10:12-16 almost word for word. Used here, the praise of the Creator is set against Judah's idols. Used against Babylon, it announces that the empire's gods and the workshops behind them will perish. One hymn serves both as a warning to Judah and as comfort for the exiles.

The psalm lists the idols' useless mouths, eyes and ears, ends with 'nor is there breath in their mouths,' and then warns that those who make them become like them. It shows the same worship tradition from which Jeremiah draws his satire and gives the moral he leaves unspoken.

The prophet mocks the man who says to wood, 'Awake!' and says there is 'no breath in it at all.' Both Habakkuk and Jeremiah ridicule overlaid wood and silver as lifeless, and both place the comparison before the point that the LORD is in His holy temple.

Babylon's gods crouch on the backs of tired animals, are lifted to the shoulder and set in place, and do not answer when called. This matches Jeremiah 10:5 and gives the other half of the contrast: Isaiah has the LORD say that He, by contrast, carries His people from birth to grey hair.

The fathers 'followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves.' This early charge explains the satire of chapter 10. The idols are worthless, and so is the nation that has been shaped by them. The two verses use the same root for worthless.

Moses warns Israel not to be enticed to worship the sun, moon and stars that the LORD has apportioned to all the nations. That is the background to Jeremiah 10:2, where the omens in the sky terrify the nations. The law had already marked the heavens as creation and not as deity.

Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You, for they have devoured Jacob. These words are nearly identical to Jeremiah 10:25, so either one borrowed from the other or both use a stock lament. The shared prayer shows how the exile and the destruction of Jerusalem were taken up into Israel's worship.

A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps. This verse says in proverb form what Jeremiah says in prayer in 10:23. The same Hebrew verb for establishing the step appears in both, which suggests that Jeremiah is drawing on wisdom teaching when he confesses his helplessness.

At Lystra Paul tells a crowd to turn from worthless things to the living God who made heaven, earth and sea. He uses Jeremiah's own pair of themes, worthless and living, and shows that the argument of Jeremiah 10 still works when the audience has never read the prophets.

Conversion is described as turning to God from idols to serve the living and true God. Jeremiah 10:10 calls the LORD both true and living, and Paul gives these two adjectives as the content of what the Thessalonians turned to. The church sees itself in the position Jeremiah wanted the nations to take.

All things were created through Christ and for Him, and in Him all things hold together. The praise of the LORD as Maker of heaven and earth in Jeremiah 10:12 is here applied to the Son, which shows how the apostles read the Old Testament's creation hymns as speaking of the one God now revealed in Christ.

Believers are told not to take lightly the Lord's discipline, since the Lord disciplines those He loves. This New Testament text explains why Jeremiah can ask for correction with confidence: discipline from God is treated as the sign of a father's love, which is why Jeremiah asks for it to be just and not angry.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 1 and 2 give the pattern that this chapter defends: a God who makes the heavens and the earth by speaking and who places humanity in His world as His image bearers. The first act of rebellion in Genesis 3 was already an exchange, believing a voice that was not God's. Idolatry is the same exchange made visible. Paul's account of fallen humanity in Romans 1:23 describes people swapping the glory of the immortal God for images, which is exactly what Jeremiah describes in the carpenter's shop.

The rest of the story runs on this question of who has made all things and who deserves our trust. At the Exodus, God defeated the gods of Egypt, and Israel sang 'Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?' Exodus 15:11. In the wilderness the golden calf showed how quickly a people rescued by the living God would reach for an object, Exodus 32:1-4. The kings, and above all Manasseh, filled the land with altars. Jeremiah arrives at the end of this history. His mockery is the voice of a God who has watched His people choose the nothing over the Someone for centuries, and who is preparing to remove them from the land for it.

But the chapter looks forward as well. Its confidence that the idols 'will perish from this earth' is taken up by Isaiah, who sees the idols carried off into captivity, Isaiah 46:1-2, and by Jeremiah himself in 16:19-20, where the nations come from the ends of the earth and confess that their fathers inherited only lies. The Portion of Jacob will be shared. The apostles then go out with this argument, telling Gentiles to turn from worthless things to the living God, Acts 14:15, and the church is formed of people who once served idols, 1 Thessalonians 1:9.

The story completes where the problem began. In the new creation the voice that opens Revelation 4:11 sings that God created all things and that by His will they exist, and the nations bring their glory into a city lit by God and the Lamb, Revelation 21:23-26. Nothing there is carried. Nothing is nailed down. The living God dwells with His people and no creature, human or heavenly, takes His place.

sermon.title: Acceptable Worship, Part Two
sermon.why: Begg preaches directly on Jeremiah 10:1-16, showing that understanding the true object of worship, the living God as He has revealed Himself, is what distinguishes acceptable worship from the idolatry this chapter exposes.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah say idols are ultimately unable to do?

options.text: Speak, walk on their own, or do any harm or good.
options.note: Verse 5 lists all of these limitations plainly.

options.text: Be decorated with silver and gold.
options.note: The text describes idols as commonly decorated this way; that is not their limitation.

options.text: Be carved from wood by a craftsman.
options.note: This describes how idols are made, not a limitation being mocked.

options.text: Be transported from one region to another.
options.note: Close to the point about being carried, but the text's emphasis is on total powerlessness, not merely portability.

quiz.q: According to verses 12-13, what has the LORD done that no idol can do?

options.text: Made the earth by His power, established the world by wisdom, and commands the storehouses of wind and rain.
options.note: Verses 12-13 credit the LORD alone with creation and control of the weather.

options.text: Set up altars in every city of Judah.
options.note: That describes Judah's idolatrous practice, condemned elsewhere in Jeremiah, not the LORD's unique work here.

options.text: Been carved by a skilled goldsmith.
options.note: That describes how idols are made, the exact opposite of the LORD's uncreated nature.

options.text: Been imported from Tarshish and Uphaz.
options.note: That describes the materials used for idols, not an act of the LORD.

quiz.q: What title does verse 16 give to the LORD in contrast to the idols?

options.text: The Portion of Jacob, the Maker of all things, the LORD of Hosts.
options.note: Verse 16 names Him this way, directly opposed to the man made idols described earlier.

options.text: The craftsman of Tarshish.
options.note: This phrase describes idol makers, not the LORD.

options.text: The scarecrow of the nations.
options.note: That image is used mockingly of the idols themselves, not of the LORD.

options.text: The King of the goldsmiths.
options.note: The chapter does call Him King of nations, verse 7, but this specific title is not used; the actual title in verse 16 concerns Jacob's inheritance.

quiz.q: How does Jeremiah describe the coming exile in verses 19-20?

options.text: As a tent destroyed with its ropes snapped and no one left to pitch it again.
options.note: Verse 20 uses this exact image of a collapsed, abandoned tent.

options.text: As a wedding feast interrupted by joyful news.
options.note: The imagery here is of devastation and loss, not celebration.

options.text: As a harvest gathered in abundance.
options.note: The image is one of loss and ruin, not abundance.

options.text: As a fortified city that withstands every siege.
options.note: The passage speaks of the land being besieged and its inhabitants scattered, not of successful resistance.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah ask for in his prayer in verses 23-24?

options.text: That the LORD correct him with justice rather than in anger, since no one directs his own steps.
options.note: Verses 23-24 record this exact humble request.

options.text: That he be spared from all discipline entirely.
options.note: Jeremiah does not ask to avoid correction, but asks that it come with justice, not destructive anger.

options.text: That God pour out wrath on Judah immediately.
options.note: That request appears in verse 25 concerning the nations, not as Jeremiah's personal plea in verses 23-24.

options.text: That his own wisdom be sufficient to direct his path.
options.note: Jeremiah actually confesses the opposite, that a man's way is not his own, verse 23.

questions: Jeremiah mocks idols that must be carried because they cannot walk. What things do you find yourself carrying, propping up, or anxiously maintaining that should instead be trusting you?
The LORD alone made the heavens and the earth by His power and wisdom. How does remembering this reshape your view of the pressures or fears you are carrying today?
Jeremiah confesses that no one who walks directs his own steps. Where are you tempted to act as though your life is fully in your own control?
Jeremiah asks to be corrected with justice, not in anger. How do you typically respond when God disciplines or corrects you, with trust in His character or with fear of His wrath?
John's Gospel echoes this chapter's praise of the Creator to describe Christ. How does seeing Jesus as the living God who made all things change the way you worship Him this week?

translationNotes.note: The image of scarecrows in a cucumber patch, or field, was a common ancient Near Eastern comparison for something propped up and harmless in appearance but utterly powerless in reality.
Tarshish and Uphaz are both associated with prized sources of precious metal in the ancient world; naming them underscores the costliness lavished on objects that remain, in the end, worthless.
This single verse is written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew, unusual within the chapter; it may have functioned as a memorable, quotable proverb for use even among Aramaic speaking exiles.
